entries.clue: Take two buses back – one interminable, that’s about right – to outskirts (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The clue's plural 'outskirts' stands for the singular SUBURB: a suburb is the town's outskirts.

indicatorNotes.back: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so each bus is read from its last letter to its first
indicatorNotes.interminable: without its end: the second bus loses its S
indicatorNotes.that’s about: the shortened bus goes around the next letter

blocks.note: take two BUSes; the first, turned back
the other BUS cut to BU, then turned back
R = right, placed inside UB to make URB

annotation.surface: A commuter changes buses twice to reach the edge of town.
annotation.walkthrough: Both buses are turned around; only the second is also docked and wrapped around R.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the residential districts on a city's edge are its outskirts.

entries.clue: Banksy’s materials: stone – and pencils? Not principally (8)

indicatorNotes.Not principally: drop the principal, i.e. first, letter

blocks.note: st = stone, the British unit of weight
PENCILS without its first letter

annotation.surface: A list of the street artist's kit: rock and pencils.
annotation.walkthrough: Banksy, the anonymous British street artist, sprays through cut stencils. A stone is 14 pounds, abbreviated ST.
annotation.definitionFit: Banksy's graffiti is made by spraying paint through stencils.

entries.clue: Bit of hubbub – a din – a geezer offering banter (8)

indicatorNotes.Bit of: the answer is a bit of the words that follow

blocks.note: hubBUB A DIN A GEezer

annotation.surface: A noisy bloke in a pub makes a racket while cracking jokes.
annotation.walkthrough: The dashes break up the run of letters; ignore them and read straight across. A geezer is British slang for a man.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, borrowed from French: witty, teasing talk.

entries.clue: Take apart so as to understand Lenurb? (7-8)

annotation.definition: Take apart so as to understand

blocks.clueFragment: Take apart so as to understand
blocks.note: to dismantle a product to learn how it was made
BRUNEL, the engineer, written in reverse

annotation.surface: A puzzle about decoding a strange word.
annotation.walkthrough: Isambard Kingdom Brunel was a great Victorian British engineer; spell his name backwards and you get the nonsense word, a literally reversed engineer.
annotation.definitionFit: To reverse-engineer is to take something apart to see how it works.

entries.clue: Envisages crumbly pie crust (8)

indicatorNotes.crumbly: the crust crumbles, so its letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: Someone dreams of a flaky pastry top.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Envisages' is a verb, so the answer is the verb 'pictures', not the noun.
annotation.definitionFit: To picture something is to envisage it.

entries.clue: Greek character included in audiotape (4)

indicatorNotes.included in: the answer is included in the next word

blocks.note: letters four to seven of the word

annotation.surface: A figure from Greece turns up on a cassette recording.
annotation.walkthrough: The Greek letter sits in plain view: audIOTApe.
annotation.definitionFit: Iota is the ninth letter of the Greek alphabet.

entries.clue: It’s safe to chase articles needing rewriting (3,5,2,5)

indicatorNotes.needing rewriting: the letters need to be written again in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

annotation.surface: A journalist is told it's fine to go after stories that need redrafting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Articles' looks like A, AN and THE, but here it is simply eight letters of fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: "The coast is clear" means there is no danger now.

entries.clue: Whispering sound Bertrand heard (6)

indicatorNotes.heard: the name as heard, not as spelt

blocks.note: Bertrand Russell, the British philosopher

annotation.surface: A philosopher catches a faint noise.
annotation.walkthrough: Say Russell out loud and it matches the answer; the surface makes Bertrand the listener, not the sound.
annotation.definitionFit: A rustle is a soft, whispering noise, like leaves or paper.

entries.clue: Framed élite soldiers? That man had (6)

blocks.note: the Special Air Service, Britain's special forces regiment
HE'D = he had

annotation.surface: Someone was stitched up by special forces; he had been framed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Framed' sounds like a false accusation, but it means fitted with a sash, the frame of a sash window.
annotation.definitionFit: A sashed window is one set in sliding frames, or sashes.

entries.clue: Object: Everyman has salad (6)

blocks.note: an end = an object or aim
the setter says I'VE = I have

annotation.surface: The setter protests about being served salad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Object' reads as a verb of protest; here it is a noun meaning goal. The setter's name stands for I.
annotation.definitionFit: Endive is a bitter leaf used in salads.

entries.clue: Emphasizes anxieties (8)

blocks.note: a verb: lays weight on a point
a plural noun: pressures and worries

annotation.surface: Someone dwells on their worries.
annotation.walkthrough: One word, two parts of speech: a verb in the first half, a plural noun in the second.
annotation.definitionFit: To stress is to emphasize, and stresses are worries.

entries.clue: Classical musician reworked her opus (7)

indicatorNotes.reworked: the letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A composer revises her piece.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Classical' means from ancient Greece and Rome, not the concert-hall sense the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: Orpheus was the legendary Greek musician who charmed all with his lyre.

entries.clue: Uncooperative? Quite the opposite! (8)

blocks.note: perversely awkward, as in 'Mary, Mary, quite ...'
the retort 'on the ...!' used to deny something

annotation.surface: Someone is accused of being difficult and denies it.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half reads as a retort, but it is itself a definition: contrary means opposite.
annotation.definitionFit: Contrary means both perversely awkward and opposite.

entries.clue: Seaman perhaps on leave, a rest (6)

blocks.note: go = leave
A as printed, then LIE = rest, as in lie down

annotation.surface: A sailor on shore leave takes a break.
annotation.walkthrough: David Seaman was England's goalkeeper in the 1990s; the surface makes him a sailor.
annotation.definitionFit: Seaman kept goal for Arsenal and England, so he is an example of a goalie.

entries.clue: Not unknown for Hazel to follow hiphop artist (7)

indicatorNotes.Not unknown for: remove an unknown, Z, from the word
indicatorNotes.to follow: the shortened name comes after the next piece

blocks.note: rap is the vocal style of hip hop
HAZEL without Z, an unknown in algebra

annotation.surface: Hazel is a well-known name trailing a rapper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hiphop artist' looks like one phrase, but the definition is just 'artist'. Algebra's unknowns are X, Y and Z.
annotation.definitionFit: Raphael was a painter of the Italian High Renaissance.

entries.clue: Heartless hello – daggers brandished – daggers drawn (11)

annotation.definitionNote: Both are used after 'at': at loggerheads, at daggers drawn.

indicatorNotes.Heartless: remove the heart, the middle letter
indicatorNotes.brandished: the daggers are waved about, so the letters move

blocks.note: HELLO without its middle L
the first daggers, anagram fodder with HELO, 11 letters

annotation.surface: A curt greeting, then knives come out in a fight.
annotation.walkthrough: The first 'daggers' is fodder; the second, with 'drawn', is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom swap: both phrases follow 'at' and mean locked in bitter hostility.

entries.clue: You can’t buy those who’ve betrayed their principles (4-4)

blocks.note: sold-out events, with no tickets left
people who have sold out

annotation.surface: Integrity can't be bought, so traitors are something you can't buy.
annotation.walkthrough: The irony: sell-outs are exactly the people who have been bought.
annotation.definitionFit: A sell-out is both a fully sold event and a person who abandons principle for gain.

entries.clue: In resort, easiest to be bored by island (in my opinion) (2,1,3,2)

indicatorNotes.to be bored by: a hole is bored in the letters and the island goes in

blocks.note: EASIEST rearranged
I = island, bored into the letters between E and T

annotation.surface: An opinion that the simplest holiday resort is a dull one on an island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Resort' reads as a holiday destination; as re-sort it tells you to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom swap: two everyday phrases for introducing a personal view.

entries.clue: Misbehaviour characteristic of the 2000s, you say? (11)

indicatorNotes.you say: what you say, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: the 2000s are nicknamed the noughties; -ness makes it a quality

annotation.surface: A claim that bad behaviour defined the first decade of this century.
annotation.walkthrough: The decade 2000–2009 is called the noughties because its years begin 200-, nought being zero.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually for a child's mischief.

entries.clue: Tom likes this brief sleep, a becoming one (6)

blocks.note: a catnap is a short doze
the A turns into I, one

annotation.surface: Tom enjoys a becoming little snooze.
annotation.walkthrough: Tom is a male cat, not a person. 'Becoming' looks like 'flattering', but here it means turning into.
annotation.definitionFit: Catnip is a plant whose scent cats adore.

entries.clue: The solver: hazard, certainly (3,3)

blocks.note: the solver is you, reading the clue
to hazard = to bet or venture

annotation.surface: A warning that the puzzler is certainly at risk.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hazard' reads as a danger, but the verb sense, to venture a guess or a stake, is the one in play.
annotation.definitionFit: "You bet!" is an informal way of saying certainly.

entries.clue: A professor is Greek, that’s lovely (6)

blocks.note: as printed
a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge, is called a don
as printed

annotation.surface: An admirer praises a professor who is Greek.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma splits the definition oddly: it means a Greek who is lovely.
annotation.definitionFit: Adonis was the beautiful youth of Greek myth, loved by Aphrodite.

entries.clue: Poirot’s one that’s been had, by Jupiter (8)

annotation.definition: one that’s been had, by Jupiter

blocks.note: Hercule Poirot, Agatha Christie's Belgian detective
the possessive S joins on

annotation.surface: Poirot, exclaiming by Jove, has been duped.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Been had' sounds like being fooled, but means being fathered: Hercules was a son of Jupiter. 'By Jupiter' looks like an oath.
annotation.definitionFit: In Roman myth Hercules was the son Jupiter fathered on Alcmene.

entries.clue: Priest raised sick in France? Ace (4)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, lifted up means written bottom to top

blocks.note: mal is French for ill
A = ace, on playing cards

annotation.surface: A cleric is taken ill on a trip to France.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In France' asks for the French word; the MAL is then flipped because this is a down clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A lama is a Buddhist priest or monk in Tibet.

entries.clue: Posh comedian? I won’t react (5,3)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition speaks as the thing itself: a noble gas says it won't react.

blocks.note: posh = aristocratic
someone who's a gas is great fun, a real laugh

annotation.surface: An upper-class comic's jokes fall flat on a stony-faced listener.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I won't react' reads as an unmoved audience, but it is chemistry: noble gases are inert.
annotation.definitionFit: Noble gases such as neon and argon hardly react with anything.

entries.clue: Act as inspiration for puzzle (6)

blocks.note: to act as = to be
a muse inspires an artist

annotation.surface: Someone serves as the spark for a crossword.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Puzzle' looks like a noun; here it is a verb, to baffle.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to leave someone bewildered.

entries.clue: Perpetual child’s play (5,3)

blocks.note: the boy who never grows up
J. M. Barrie's 1904 stage play

annotation.surface: Something is as easy as child's play forever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Child's play' looks like one idiom for something easy; split it, and the possessive ties the child to his own play.
annotation.definitionFit: Peter Pan never grows up, and his story began as a play.

entries.clue: Please raise one’s Stein in toasting, primarily! (6)

annotation.definition: Please raise one’s Stein in toasting, primarily!

indicatorNotes.primarily: take the first letter of each word

blocks.clueFragment: Please raise one’s Stein in toasting
blocks.note: Please Raise One's Stein In Toasting

annotation.surface: A German drinking host urges everyone to lift their beer mugs.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: it describes what you do when you say the toast. A Stein is a German beer mug.
annotation.definitionFit: Prosit is the German toast, like cheers.
